column1: Supply and demand shocks in the COVID‑19 pandemic: An industry and occupation perspective

The thesis titled Supply and demand shocks in the COVID-19 pandemic: An industry and occupation perspective by R. Maria del Rio-Chanona  Penny Mealy  Anton Pichler  François Lafond  and J. Doyne Farmer  provides a detailed analysis of the economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on the U.S. economy  focusing on supply and demand shocks at the level of individual occupations and industries. The authors classify industries as essential or non-essential and develop a Remote Labor Index to assess the ability of different occupations to work from home  which helps in analyzing the supply shock. Demand shocks are evaluated based on a study by the US Congressional Budget Office on the effects of a severe influenza epidemic. The study predicts that these shocks could threaten around 22% of the U.S. GDP  jeopardize 24% of jobs  and reduce total wage income by 17%. At the industry level  sectors like transport are expected to be constrained by demand shocks  while manufacturing  mining  and services are more likely to face supply constraints. Entertainment  restaurants  and tourism are anticipated to experience significant supply and demand shocks. At the occupational level  high-wage occupations are relatively insulated from these shocks  whereas low-wage occupations are more vulnerable. The authors emphasize that their results represent first-order shocks and anticipate that these will be amplified by feedback effects within the production network. The study aims to provide clarity on the supply and demand shocks caused by public health measures and changes in consumer preferences due to the pandemic. It estimates supply-side reductions due to the closure of non-essential industries and the inability of workers to perform their activities at home  alongside demand-side changes due to increased demand for healthcare and reduced demand for goods or services that pose a risk of infection. The authors stress that the predicted shocks should not be interpreted as the overall economic impact of the pandemic  as second-order effects  such as reduced demand from income losses and supply chain disruptions  could further amplify the initial shocks. The study also compares supply and demand shocks to determine which is the more significant constraint on output in various industries. The authors propose a methodology for estimating the feasibility of remote work based on work activities  identify essential industries  and compare estimated supply shocks to demand shocks. They highlight the importance of understanding the interplay between supply and demand shocks to assess the immediate economic impact of the pandemic. The study concludes that most of the first-order impact on the economy will be due to an inability of people to work rather than to consume  but anticipates larger second-order negative impacts on demand as wages drop. The authors intend to present results from a macroeconomic model in the future to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the pandemic's economic impact.
